Little's test for data missing completely at random

Source: R/dsc.R
mcartst.Rd

Tests the MCAR assumption: that whether a value is missing is unrelated to any value in the data, observed or not.

Usage

mcartst(data, maxit = 500L, tol = 1e-07)

# S3 method for class 'mcartst'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame or numeric matrix. Non-numeric columns are dropped with a warning, since the statistic is defined on moments.

maxit

Whole number, default 500: the maximum number of EM iterations.

tol

Number, default 1e-7: EM stops when the largest absolute change in any mean or covariance entry between iterations falls below it.

x

A result of mcartst().

...

Not used.

Value

A list of class c("mcartst", "list"): statistic, df, logpvalue (the log of p_value, finite where p_value underflows to 0), p_value, npat (distinct missingness patterns), nused (rows in the patterns that entered the statistic), nvars (columns used), iterations (EM iterations), mu (named ML means), sigma (ML covariance matrix), and note (a caveat when the test is degenerate or a pattern was skipped, else NA). With complete data df is 0 and p_value is NA – there is nothing to test.

Details

The assumption matters because it is what licenses the easy options. Dropping incomplete rows is unbiased under MCAR and biased otherwise; mean imputation understates variance under MCAR and distorts the centre as well otherwise. A small p-value here says the easy options are not available. Run it on the numeric columns of a table before deciding how to handle its missing values.

Rows are grouped by their pattern of missingness. If missingness is unrelated to the values, then each pattern's observed-variable means should agree with the overall estimates, up to sampling error. The statistic sums those disagreements, $$d^2 = \sum_j n_j (\bar{x}_j - \hat{\mu}_j)' \hat{\Sigma}_j^{-1} (\bar{x}_j - \hat{\mu}_j),$$ over the variables observed in pattern \(j\), and is compared with a chi-square distribution on \(\sum_j p_j - p\) degrees of freedom.

The overall \(\hat\mu\) and \(\hat\Sigma\) are the MAXIMUM-LIKELIHOOD estimates under multivariate normality WITH the missing data, obtained by expectation-maximisation – not the complete-case estimates, which would already embed the bias the test is looking for.

A large p-value is NOT evidence that the data are MCAR; it is a failure to detect a departure, and the test has little power on small samples or with many patterns. The test also assumes multivariate normality, so on markedly non-normal columns a rejection may be telling you about the distribution rather than the missingness. Neither this test nor any other can distinguish missing-at-random from missing-NOT-at-random, because that distinction depends on the values that were never observed.

Collinear or constant columns are refused rather than worked around: the likelihood is degenerate there, and the EM step's eigenvalue floor would otherwise return a statistic governed by that floor instead of by the data. Columns that are entirely missing and rows with no observed value are dropped before the test. If EM has not converged after maxit iterations the last estimates are used; iterations then equals maxit.

Errors: data neither a data frame nor a matrix; fewer than two numeric columns, or fewer than two usable rows or columns after the drops; collinear or constant columns (smallest eigenvalue of the correlation matrix at most \(10^{-8}\) times the largest, or a standard deviation at most \(10^{-12}\) times the column's largest absolute value); EM estimates that cannot be inverted. Non-numeric columns are dropped with a warning.

References

Little, R. J. A. (1988). A test of missing completely at random for multivariate data with missing values. Journal of the American Statistical Association 83(404), 1198-1202. doi:10.1080/01621459.1988.10478722

Dempster, A. P., Laird, N. M. and Rubin, D. B. (1977). Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 39(1), 1-38.

See also

misspat for the patterns themselves, misssmry for the rates.

Examples

set.seed(1)
n <- 300
x <- stats::rnorm(n) # simulated
y <- x + stats::rnorm(n)

# Missing completely at random: a coin flip decides, so the test
# should not reject.
mcar <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
mcar$y[sample(n, 90)] <- NA
mcartst(mcar)
#> Little's MCAR test: no departure from MCAR detected
#>   Statistic 1.094 on 1 df, p = 0.296
#>   Patterns 2, variables 2, rows used 300, EM iterations 13

# Missing depending on the OTHER, observed variable: not MCAR, and
# detectable, because the pattern's mean of x is shifted.
mar <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)
mar$y[x > 0.4] <- NA
mcartst(mar)
#> Little's MCAR test: MCAR rejected: the missingness is related to the data
#>   Statistic 180.118 on 1 df, p = 4.57e-41
#>   Patterns 2, variables 2, rows used 300, EM iterations 69

# Complete data has one pattern and nothing to test.
mcartst(data.frame(a = x, b = y))$df
#> [1] 0

# A duplicated column makes the likelihood degenerate, and is refused.
dup <- mcar
dup$x2 <- dup$x
try(mcartst(dup))
#> Error : mcartst: the columns are collinear (or one is constant), so the multivariate normal likelihood Little's test is built on is degenerate. Drop the redundant column(s) first -- topcors() and drpconst() will find them.
